plain: Claude Code is a helper that works inside your computer, not inside a webpage. You talk to it in English, tell it what you want to build, and it creates the folders, writes the files, tests them, and fixes them when they break. The difference from a normal chat is that it doesn't hand you back text for you to copy: it does the work itself, on your hard drive, in front of you, asking permission every time it's about to touch something. It's the difference between a handyman explaining over the phone how to assemble the wardrobe and a handyman showing up at your house with the toolbox.

account.free: There's no free plan. The free web version of Claude works for chatting, but it doesn't open Claude Code. You need one of two things. One: a subscription. The Pro plan runs about 20 dollars a month and gives you Claude Code with short limits (fine for learning and small projects); the Max plans, meant for working hours on end, range from about 100 to about 200 dollars a month. See the exact prices in dollars with tax at claude.ai before paying, under Settings then Billing: check them there, they change and I don't want to give you a stale figure. Two: an Anthropic console account with balance, billed by usage. I don't recommend that second option to start with: a long afternoon with the big model can eat 10 or 20 dollars without you noticing, while the subscription stops you on its own once you hit the limit. With a subscription there are two caps: one every few hours and one weekly. When you hit them, you wait.
steps: Create the account and choose a plan

Go to claude.ai and click Sign up. Once your email is in, go to the bottom left where your name shows, and look for Upgrade plan. Choose Pro to start. Note: the subscription renews itself every month until you cancel it by hand from Settings then Billing. Nobody warns you the day before.

Claude Code installs through a tool that comes inside Node.js. Go to nodejs.org, click the big green button that says LTS (long-term support version, the stable one), and click Next all the way through without changing anything. To check it: open PowerShell (Windows key, type powershell, Enter), type node --version and press Enter. It should show something like v20.11.0. If it shows a number below 18, update it.

Go to git-scm.com and click Download for Windows. Install it with the default options. It's useful for two things: Claude Code relies on tools that come with this package, and Git is your real undo button. Without this, when something breaks there's no way back.

In PowerShell type: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code and press Enter. It takes a minute or two and prints a lot of text; that's normal. When it's done, type claude --version. If it gives you back a number, you're set. There's also an installer on claude.ai that doesn't need Node.js; if you use it, copy the command from the official page itself, never from a video or a forum.
Create the project folder outside OneDrive

Open File Explorer, go to the C: drive and create a folder called projects, and inside it another one named after your idea, no spaces or accents: for example C:\projects\ceramics-site. Outside OneDrive and outside the Desktop, seriously: OneDrive syncs files while they're being written and causes really strange errors you'll run into without knowing why.
Start Claude Code inside that folder

Right-click the folder and choose Open in Terminal. A black window opens with your folder's path written at the start of the line. Type claude and press Enter. The first time it asks about color theme and then how you want to sign in: choose the subscription account option, not the console one. The browser opens, click Authorize, and go back to the black window.

Type /status and press Enter: it tells you the version, which account you're signed in with, and what plan you have. Type /doctor: it checks the install and tells you if anything's missing. And press Shift+Tab twice: a notice should appear at the bottom saying you're in plan mode. If you've seen those three things, it's set up.
account.warning: This isn't a chat. It's a program with hands: it reads your files, writes new ones, deletes, installs things, and runs commands on your actual computer. What it deletes from there doesn't go to the recycle bin. That's why it asks permission before every action, and why you have to read what it's asking before saying yes. Never start it with the option that skips all permissions (you'll see it written as --dangerously-skip-permissions, which literally means skip permissions dangerously): it exists for isolated servers, not for your laptop with your photos and your accounting on it. And always open it inside a specific project folder, never in C:\Users\your-name, because from there it can see everything you have.

first: Press Shift+Tab twice until the bottom says you're in plan mode. In that mode Claude investigates, asks questions, and proposes a plan, but doesn't touch a single file. Always start this way.

Tell it your idea in one paragraph, plainly and without holding back: I want a one-page website for my ceramics studio in Austin, with hours, five photos, and a contact form that emails me. Press Enter.

Read the whole plan before accepting anything. If something's off, correct it in your own words (the form shouldn't ask for a phone number) and ask for the plan again. This is where the afternoon is won or lost.
Before letting it write anything, tell it this: create a git repository in this folder and make a first commit before touching anything. It's your only undo that truly holds.

Once files exist, type /init. It generates the CLAUDE.md file, which is the project's memory. Open it, read the whole thing, and edit it to your liking: it's going to read that file every new conversation.
shortcuts: Shift+Tab

Switches the permission mode and is the single most important shortcut. One press: accepts file changes without asking you one by one (fast, and dangerous if you don't know what it's doing). Two presses: plan mode, where it investigates and proposes but doesn't touch anything. You'll live between normal mode and plan mode.
Esc

Stops Claude cold in the middle of whatever it's doing, without closing the conversation. When you see it's understood something else and has already written three files, don't wait for it to finish: Esc and explain.
Esc twice in a row

Takes you back in the conversation to rewrite an earlier message of yours and continue from there, as if nothing after that had happened. Recent versions also have /rewind, which returns the files to the state they had at an earlier point. Check for it in your version with /help before relying on it: it's not a replacement for git.
/clear

Empties the conversation and starts fresh, keeping the project. Use it every time you switch tasks. A long conversation full of failed attempts makes it lose track and repeat mistakes you'd already solved.
/compact

Summarizes the entire conversation into a short text and continues with that, to free up space. This is what you want when you've been on the same task for two hours and can't start from scratch. You can tell it what to keep: /compact keep the design decisions and the form problem.
# at the start of the line

Everything you write after the hash gets saved into the project's memory (the CLAUDE.md file) instead of being a normal message. Example: # prices always in dollars, tax included. It's the quick way to make sure a rule isn't forgotten tomorrow.
@ and a file name
Points it to a specific file and autocompletes as you type. Example: check @index.html and tell me why the menu is misaligned on mobile. Saves it having to search, and gets it right more often.
! at the start of the line
Runs a system command directly, without Claude interpreting anything. Example: !dir to see what files are there. Useful for quickly checking something yourself without spending conversation.
Up arrow
Recalls the last thing you typed. When a long request didn't come out how you wanted, up arrow, change two words, and relaunch it instead of retyping the whole thing.
/help and /status

/help lists every slash command your installed version has, which is the only reliable list because they change often. /status tells you which account you're signed in with, which plan, and which folder you're working in. Check it whenever something smells off.
daily: Start in plan mode (Shift+Tab twice) and don't leave it until the plan looks right to you. Reading a plan in plain English costs two minutes; undoing forty badly made files costs an afternoon.
Keep a short, bossy CLAUDE.md at the project root. It reads it at the start of every conversation. Without that file you repeat the same instructions every day and some get forgotten.
Type /clear between different tasks. Finishing the contact form and starting the photo gallery are two conversations, not one.

Ask for a commit every time something works: make a commit with this, it's working now. These are your save points. When something breaks, tell it go back to the last commit and you get back a project that worked.

When something looks wrong on screen, take a screenshot and paste it into the window with Ctrl+V. It understands images, and describing in words that a button is three pixels too low is a waste of time.
End every request with the same tag: and tell me step by step how I test it. What I type, what I open, where I click, and what I should see. If you can't test it, you don't know if it's done.
To pick up yesterday's work, start with claude --continue (resumes that folder's last conversation) or type /resume to choose from a list. Don't start from scratch explaining everything again.

templates.name: CLAUDE.md for someone who doesn't code
templates.what: The project's memory file. Claude reads the whole thing at the start of every conversation, so it's where you put the rules you never want to repeat: speak to me in English, don't delete anything without asking, warn me before anything that costs money. Works for any project: website, shop, app, or assistant.
templates.how: 1) In the Claude Code window, type /init: it generates a first CLAUDE.md by looking at what's in the folder. 2) Type /memory to open and edit it. 3) Delete what it put there and paste this, filling in the brackets. 4) Save. 5) Type /clear and start a new conversation: ask it to summarize its working rules back to you. If it repeats them correctly, it's reading them. Every time you discover a new rule the hard way, add it with # at the start of the line.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
What you call it: ceramics-site, cheese-shop, appointment-book
[ONE SENTENCE: what it does and for whom]
One-page website for my ceramics studio, so people can see hours and write to me
[WHO WILL USE IT]
Customers aged 30 to 60, almost all on mobile
[HOW I'LL KNOW IT WORKS]
When I receive a test email sent from the form
[COMMAND TO START IT]
Leave it as pending until it exists, and ask it to fill it in once it does
[WHERE IT GETS PUBLISHED]
Where it's going to live on the internet. If you don't know yet, write undecided
templates.code:
# Project: [PROJECT NAME]

## Who I am
I don't code and I'm not going to learn. I'm building this by talking to you.
Always talk to me in plain English. Translate every technical word in parentheses the first time you use it.

## What this is
[ONE SENTENCE: what it does and for whom]
Who will use it: [WHO WILL USE IT]
It will be done when: [HOW I'LL KNOW IT WORKS]

## Working rules
- Before touching more than one file, show me the plan and wait for me to type ok.
- Small changes. One thing at a time.
- After every change that works, make a commit with the message in English.
- Never delete files or folders without asking me first.
- Don't install anything new without telling me what it is, why it's needed, and whether it's free.
- Never write passwords or keys inside the code: those go in the .env file.
- If something is going to cost money (a domain, hosting, an external service), stop and tell me before continuing.
- I prefer the boring, common solution over the trendy one. It should still have answers online a year from now.

## How you report back
- When done, write three lines: what you changed, in which file, and what I need to do to see it.
- Always give me the test step: what I type, what I open, where I click, and what I should see.
- If you're stuck halfway or unsure, say so in those words. Don't make it up.

## How this gets started
Install: [pending]
Start: [COMMAND TO START IT]
View in browser: [pending]

## Decisions made (don't change without asking)
- Language for everything the user sees: English.
- Prices in dollars, tax included.
- Published on: [WHERE IT GETS PUBLISHED]

## Things we already tried that did NOT work
- (empty: log things here as they go wrong)

templates.name: Your own slash command: /review
templates.what: A command of your own, not built in. You type /review and it hands you an audit of the project in plain English: what it does today, what's broken or half-done, what real risks there are, and what to do next. It's the answer to reviewing without being able to read code, and you'll use it at the end of every session.
templates.how: 1) Ask Claude Code this: create the folder .claude/commands at the project root and inside it a file called review.md with the content I'm about to paste. 2) Paste the text below. 3) Type /help and confirm /review shows up in the list. 4) Type /review and wait. If you want to point it at something specific, type /review the contact form: that text is fed into where it says ARGUMENTS. To have it in every project, put the file in the .claude/commands folder under your user account instead of the project's.
fill: The file name
review.md, and the command becomes /review. If you call it audit.md, it becomes /audit
The description line
What you want to show up next to the command when you type /help
Block 3, RISKS
Add your own: if your project takes payments or stores client data, say so explicitly there
templates.code:
---
description: Reviews the project and explains it in plain English
---

You are my reviewer. I don't code. Review the current state of the project and answer in plain English, in four short blocks with no untranslated jargon.

1. WHAT IT DOES TODAY: in three sentences, what this is capable of right now, as if explaining it to my mother.

2. BROKEN OR HALF-DONE: list of what doesn't work, what's unfinished, and what fakes working (placeholder data, buttons that go nowhere, forms that don't actually send anything). Mark each line: visible from outside / not visible from outside.

3. REAL RISKS: passwords or keys written inside the code, unprotected personal data, things that could start costing money without warning, and files that shouldn't be uploaded to the internet. If you find none, say so in those words: I found none.

4. WHAT'S NEXT: the three things you'd start with tomorrow, ranked by how much it hurts if not done. One sentence of why for each.

Rules: don't change a single file, this is read-only. If you couldn't check something, say so instead of assuming it. No congratulating me: I want the list of what's missing.

Pay special attention to this, if I give it: $ARGUMENTS

templates.name: Saved permissions: .claude/settings.json
templates.what: A list of what Claude can do without asking you, what it has to check with you first, and what it can never do. Stops it interrupting you every fifteen seconds to ask permission to read a file, while still keeping the door closed on deleting things and reading your keys. It's the middle ground between saying yes a hundred times a day and skipping permissions entirely, which you must not do.
templates.how: 1) Ask it: create the file .claude/settings.json at the project root with this content, and paste the text below. 2) Exit with Ctrl+C twice and re-enter by typing claude: permissions load on startup. 3) Type /permissions to see the list as it understood it. If a line doesn't show up, it's written wrong. 4) When you get tired of saying yes to a specific command, add it yourself to the allow list, never on the sly with the skip-everything option.
fill: The allow lines with npm
Swap them for your project's real commands. If you don't use npm, ask Claude to adapt them for you
The deny lines with .env
Always keep these. They're what stops your keys from entering the conversation
Bash(git push:*) in ask
Leave it in ask: pushing to the internet is one of the few things that can't be undone
templates.code:
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Read",
      "Edit",
      "Write",
      "Bash(git status)",
      "Bash(git diff:*)",
      "Bash(git log:*)",
      "Bash(git add:*)",
      "Bash(git commit:*)",
      "Bash(npm run dev)",
      "Bash(npm run build)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(npm install:*)",
      "Bash(git push:*)",
      "WebFetch"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Bash(rm:*)",
      "Bash(rmdir:*)",
      "Bash(del:*)",
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Read(./secrets/**)"
    ]
  }
}

templates.name: Where keys go: .gitignore and .env
templates.what: Two three-line files that prevent the most expensive mistake in the whole course: accidentally publishing a password or an access key. The .gitignore is the list of what never gets uploaded to the internet. The .env is where keys live, outside the code. The .env.example is the empty copy that does get uploaded, so people know what keys are needed without revealing any of them.
templates.how: 1) As soon as you create the project, before writing a single line, ask it: create the .gitignore with this content and a .env.example file. 2) Paste the two blocks below (separated by the dashed line). 3) Copy .env.example, rename it to .env, and put your real keys there. 4) Confirm it works: ask it show me what files would be uploaded if I commit now, and confirm .env does NOT show up. If it does, don't continue until you fix it.
fill: The .env.example lines
Swap them for the keys your project actually uses. Ask Claude: tell me what keys this project needs and where they come from
The value put_your_key_here
In the .env file, your real key. In .env.example it stays as-is, empty
node_modules/ and dist/
Only apply if your project has them. Extra unused lines don't break anything
templates.code:
# ---------- file: .gitignore ----------
.env
.env.local
.env.*.local
node_modules/
dist/
build/
*.log
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
.claude/settings.local.json

# ---------- file: .env.example ----------
# Copy this file, rename it to .env, and fill in the real values.
# The .env file never gets uploaded to the internet. This one, the .example, does.
EMAIL_SENDING_KEY=put_your_key_here
PAYMENTS_KEY=put_your_key_here
DATABASE_ADDRESS=put_your_key_here

errors: claude : The term 'claude' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet, function, script file, or operable program.

Your computer can't find the program. It's almost always because you installed Claude Code with the PowerShell window already open: close it completely and open a new one. If it still fails, the install didn't finish properly: run npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code again and read the last few lines instead of skipping past them. Check first that Node.js is there: node --version should give you a number.
npm WARN EBADENGINE Unsupported engine { required: { node: '>=18' } }

Your Node.js is too old for this program. Go back to nodejs.org, download the LTS version, and install it over the old one; no need to uninstall anything. Then close PowerShell, open a new window, and repeat the Claude Code install. This warning sometimes shows up as just a WARN and lets you continue: don't ignore it, it later fails in weird, senseless ways.
Claude usage limit reached. Your limit will reset at 15:00.

You've used up your plan's quota. It's not a malfunction or your fault: the subscription has a cap every few hours and another weekly. It tells you what time you'll have it back. While you wait, use the time to read what it did and try it out by hand. If this happens daily, the fix is upgrading your plan (Max, roughly 100 dollars a month), and that's real money: measure a week before deciding.
API Error: 400 prompt is too long: 214532 tokens > 200000 maximum

The conversation no longer fits in its working memory. It has a limit and the two of you filled it. Quick fix: type /compact and continue. Real fix: type /clear when switching tasks, instead of dragging three hours of failed attempts along. Before you get here, the screen shows a warning of how much room is left: pay attention to it.
Do you want to make this edit to index.html? 1. Yes  2. Yes, allow all edits during this session  3. No, and tell Claude what to do differently (esc)

This isn't an error, it's the permission question, and it's the moment everything gets decided. 1 accepts that change. 2 accepts every file change from here to the end of the session, and it's equal parts convenient and dangerous: use it only once you've read the plan and know what it's going to do. 3 stops it and lets you write what you actually wanted. Before pressing anything, look at the green and red lines above: green is what's being added, red what's being removed.

OneDrive had the file locked while Claude was trying to write it. It happens because your project is on the Desktop or in Documents, and OneDrive syncs those folders. There's no trick: move the whole folder to C:\projects and reopen Claude Code there. Leave the project in OneDrive and you'll eat intermittent errors for weeks without understanding where they come from.
Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000

Your site is already running in another window and you're trying to start it twice in the same spot. Find the other black window and close it with Ctrl+C, or tell Claude: shut down whatever's using port 3000 and start it again. The number could be different (5173, 8000): it's the door your project shows itself through in the browser.
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git

There's no history in this folder, so there's no way back. Fix it right now: create a git repository here and make a first commit with everything that's in it. If this message shows up after three days of work, you've been three days without a safety net. Also check which folder you're in: sometimes this happens because you opened Claude Code one level above or below the project.

prompts.name: Commission a whole project from scratch, without it writing wildly
prompts.prompt:
I want us to build [WHAT IT IS: a one-page website / an online shop / a mobile app / an assistant that answers emails] for [WHO FOR: my ceramics studio in Austin / my clinic / my neighborhood association]. I don't code and I'm not going to code: you write all the code, I test and decide. Talk to me in plain English and translate every technical word the first time you use it.

Don't write a single line of code yet. First I want a plan, and I want it like this:

1. Repeat back in your own words what you've understood I want, including anything you think I want but haven't said. If you assumed something, say so out loud.
2. Ask me at most five questions: the five that would change the outcome most if I got them wrong. One at a time, not all at once.
3. Suggest the most boring, most common way to do it. Nothing trendy for the sake of being trendy: I want there to still be answers about this online a year from now.
4. Tell me what's going to cost money: domain, hosting, external services, sending emails. Name, why it's needed, and how much per month in dollars. If there's a free option that's enough to start with, tell me that too.
5. Break the work into pieces where I can see the result. Each piece has to end with something I can open, look at, and test.
6. Tell me what you need from me and when: an account somewhere, the photos, the text, the logo, a card.

What I already have: [TEXT, PHOTOS, LOGO, COLORS, DOMAIN IF YOU ALREADY HAVE ONE].
I'd like to see it working by [DATE].

Wait for me to read the plan and tell you where to start.

prompts.name: Review what it did without being able to read code
prompts.prompt:
You just finished [WHAT YOU JUST ASKED FOR]. I can't read code, so showing me the file or telling me it's done isn't useful. Explain it to me like I'm the boss paying for it, not the one coding it. Answer in this order, in plain English:

1. In three sentences and without a single untranslated word: what this does now that it didn't before.
2. Show me how to test it. Step by step: what I type in the terminal, what address I open in the browser, where I click, and what I should see on screen if it's working. Also tell me what I'd see if it weren't, so I can tell the difference.
3. List the files you touched and, next to each one, a sentence saying what that file is in real-world terms: this is the page the customer sees, this stores the orders, this sends the emails.
4. Tell me what you assumed: everything you decided on my behalf because I didn't ask about it.
5. Tell me what's fake: sample data, placeholder text, test photos, buttons that go nowhere, forms that don't actually send anything. The full list, even if it's long and looks bad.
6. Rate your confidence from 0 to 10 that this works on someone else's computer, and explain the number.

If at any point you're not sure, write I'm not sure. I'd rather have that than a nice-sounding summary. Don't congratulate me.

prompts.name: When something broke and you have no idea why
prompts.prompt:
Something broke. I can't read code, so you drive the investigation, but you'll walk me through it in plain, clear English.

What I see: [DESCRIBE WHAT'S HAPPENING: a blank screen / red text appears / the button does nothing / the page hangs and freezes].
The message that shows up, copied exactly: [PASTE THE FULL TEXT HERE, even if it's twenty lines and you don't understand any of it].
The last thing we did before it broke: [WHAT I ASKED YOU FOR, WHAT I TOUCHED MYSELF, WHAT WE INSTALLED].
System: Windows 11.

Work like this, and don't skip steps:

1. Before touching anything, tell me in one sentence what you think happened, no jargon.
2. Give me your three suspicions ranked from most to least likely, with the reason for each.
3. Start with the first and check it: look at the files and run whatever you need, but read-only, without changing anything yet. Tell me what you found.
4. Once you know the cause, propose the smallest possible fix. The smallest, not the most elegant. No rewriting half the project while you're at it.
5. Tell me what else could break because of that fix.
6. Wait for me to type go ahead.
7. After fixing it, tell me how I confirm it's fixed, and make a commit with a message in English explaining what was wrong.

If you've tried two things and still don't know, stop and tell me. I'd rather have that than you changing files hoping something works.

prompts.name: Have it write your custom CLAUDE.md
prompts.prompt:
I want you to write this project's CLAUDE.md file. It's the memory you'll read at the start of every new conversation, so it's written for you, but I need to be able to understand all of it: I don't code.

Before writing anything, look at what's already in this folder: what files exist, what it's built with, how it's installed, and how it's started. Don't assume. If you can't find the command to start it or aren't sure what something's for, ask me first.

Then write it with these sections, in English and kept short:
- What this project is and for whom, in two sentences.
- What it's built with and which decisions are already made and shouldn't be changed without asking me.
- How it's installed, how it's started, and what address it's viewed at. With the exact, copyable commands.
- How to talk to me: plain English, every technical word translated the first time, and a note that I don't code and I'm not going to.
- Working rules: plan before touching several files, small changes, commit after everything that works, never delete without asking, never keys inside the code, warn me before anything that costs money.
- What NOT to do on this project, with anything we've already learned the hard way.

Rules for the file itself: it should fit on one screen. Sentences in the imperative, no filler paragraphs. If a section doesn't apply yet, leave it with a line saying pending. Once you have it, show me the whole thing in the chat before saving it, I want to read it.

prompts.name: Before showing it to someone: what costs money and what can't be undone
prompts.prompt:
I'm about to take this out of my computer: [WHERE: I'm sending it to a client / publishing it on a domain / uploading it to an app store]. Before that I want a review of the things that can't be undone. Don't fix anything yet: lists first.

Review the whole project and answer in English, in five blocks:

1. MONEY: everything that's going to cost dollars, one-time or monthly: domain, hosting, database, sending emails, external services. Name of the service, why it's needed, how much it costs, and whether there's a free plan good enough to start with. If something only gets charged once usage grows, say so in those words and tell me at what point.
2. SECRETS: any password, key, or access data written inside a project file. Tell me which file and which line, and move it out of there into the .env file.
3. WHAT GETS UPLOADED: which files and folders would get uploaded that shouldn't. Show me the .gitignore and tell me what's missing from it.
4. PERSONAL DATA: if this collects names, emails, phone numbers, or any client data, tell me where it's stored, who can see it, and what I'm legally missing: cookie notice, privacy policy, form consent.
5. WHAT'S FAKE: placeholder text, sample photos, forms that don't send anything, test payments that don't actually charge.

Once you have the five blocks, sort them into two columns for me: what I must fix before publishing, and what can wait. Be conservative: if in doubt, put it in the first column.

words: Terminal

The black window where you give the computer commands by typing them, instead of clicking. Claude Code lives in there: no windows, no menus, no buttons. You type, press Enter, and it answers with text.
Slash command
A command that starts with a forward slash and isn't directed at Claude, but at the program. /clear, /compact, /init. You can create your own by putting a text file in the .claude/commands folder.
CLAUDE.md

The project's memory file. A plain text file Claude reads in full at the start of every conversation. This is where you put the rules you don't want to repeat every day. Created with /init and edited with /memory.
Context

Its working memory within a conversation: everything you've said to each other plus the files it's read. It's large but capped, and when it fills up it starts forgetting the beginning. That's why /clear and /compact exist.
Plan mode
A state where it investigates, asks questions, and proposes, but doesn't write or delete anything. Turned on with Shift+Tab twice. This is the mode you should make every important decision in.
Permission
The question it asks before every action with consequences: reading a file, writing it, running a command. You can answer one at a time or write the list out in advance in .claude/settings.json.
Commit

A snapshot of the whole project at a specific moment, saved to its history. It's your save point: when something breaks, you go back to the last commit and get back a project that worked. Git makes them, and you ask Claude for them by talking.
Dependency
A piece of software made by someone else that your project uses. Installing one means putting a stranger's code into your folder: that's why you ask what it is and what it's for before accepting it.
Local server (localhost)

Your project running on your own computer, so you can see it before it exists on the internet. It opens in the browser at an address like http://localhost:3000. Only you can see it, and it disappears when you close the black window.
.env file
A separate file where keys and passwords are stored, outside the code. The dot at the start makes it a hidden file. It's the only place they should be, and it never gets uploaded to the internet.
matters: Git from the first minute, before writing a single line. Claude has ways to go back within the conversation, and they're handy, but they're not a history: they're lost when you close it, they don't cover what you touch by hand, and they don't cover what runs outside it. A commit does. If you ask for commits every time something works, the worst that can happen on a bad day is losing half an hour. Without that, one Monday afternoon you ask for a small change, it gets tangled, rewrites six files, and there's no human way to recover what you had. This isn't theoretical: it happens to everyone in the second week.

Keys and passwords go in the .env file, never inside the code. And .env goes into .gitignore before it even exists. This matters because it can't be undone: if you upload a project to the internet with a key inside it, that key stays saved in the history forever, and deleting it tomorrow doesn't remove it from today's version. There are automated programs scanning exactly those spots for exactly that. If it's a key for a pay-per-use service, it can leave you a three-figure bill before you notice.

Read what it's asking before saying yes. The option to accept every change for the session is convenient and has its moment, but only after you've read the plan. And the option that skips all permissions, the one you'll see written as --dangerously-skip-permissions, isn't for you: you'd be giving a program permission to delete, install, and run whatever it wants on your computer without saying a word. Also, always open it inside the project folder. If you start it in your user folder, it can read your photos, your accounting, and everything else.

There are things you shouldn't use it for yet, and knowing that saves you grief. Anything touching real money: charges, subscriptions, card payments. Anything storing personal data: names, emails, phone numbers, ID numbers, and certainly not health data or minors' data, where data protection law asks for things an AI can't settle for you. Anything that already works and that someone's livelihood depends on: don't unleash an agent on the website that brings your brother-in-law his customers. And nothing about fixing the computer, touching system settings, or cleaning up folders. While you're learning, the worst that should happen is losing some time. Once the project outgrows that, that's when it's worth paying someone who can read code for a couple of hours.
ignore: MCP and connectors (plugging Claude Code into your database, your Figma, or your Notion). It's powerful and you'll want it someday, but every connector is another open door and one more thing that can break. First get the first website working.

Subagents (/agents), hooks, and plugins. These automate your way of working, and to automate a way of working you need to have one. Come back to this once you've had twenty sessions and notice you repeat the same thing every day.
Choosing a model with /model, vim mode, and output styles. The default is well chosen, and changing it before you can tell the difference just adds one more variable for when something goes wrong.
